signature_moments.source_phrase: It traffics in the flesh of its own children
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the sharpest compression of dynastic greed turning inward and cannibalistic.

signature_moments.moment: The universe celebrates a completed purgation with an earthquake rather than with a private inner feeling alone.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the universe celebrates with an earthquake
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It externalizes salvation into a cosmic event and makes the mountain itself morally alive.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil defines the reach of pagan wisdom by saying he can lead Dante only as far as his teaching reaches.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I shall lead him just as far as where I teach can reach
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is a compact statement of Virgil's greatness and limit at once.

signature_moments.moment: The mountain is described as so ordered that no perturbation touches it except the moral liberation of a soul.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it only trembles here when some soul feels its cleanse
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The entire environment becomes keyed to purification rather than to blind natural causation.

signature_moments.moment: Purity is measured by a will that becomes fully free enough to change dwelling place.
signature_moments.source_phrase: The will alone is proof of purity
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's central definition of purgatorial freedom.

signature_moments.moment: The soul's ascent is delayed not merely by punishment from outside but by an inward longing to continue penance.
signature_moments.source_phrase: that will was opposed by longing to do penance
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It reverses the simple external-punishment model and sets up Jiang's free-will reading.

signature_moments.moment: Purgatory is redefined as souls punishing themselves because they want to be worthy of God.
signature_moments.source_phrase: It's not God punishing us. It's we're punishing ourselves
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's sharpest free-will formulation for why purgatorial suffering exists at all.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns penance into the desire to show up at the divine meeting in your best form, like dressing for prom.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's like going to the prom
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The analogy domesticates an abstract theological point without softening its voluntary rigor.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil is said to be too real to have been merely invented and instead must be summoned.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's no way Dante could have created Virgil
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This condenses Jiang's larger claim that the poem is tapping a reality deeper than authorial fabrication.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns the scene into a study of micro-expressions carrying more truth than speech.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's all just like micro expressions
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is his method claim for why Dante can feel summoned from lived reality rather than fabricated from abstractions.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil shifts from autograph-seeking delight with Sordello to embarrassed refusal before Statius.
signature_moments.source_phrase: could you please stop just stop man just stop
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The emotional reversal sets up Jiang’s larger argument that Virgil is being exposed rather than flattered.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns Virgil into a case study in irreducible self-knowledge: you can fool the world but not yourself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's no way you can ever fool yourself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This becomes the engine of Virgil’s discomfort and Jiang’s broader psychology of bad faith.

signature_moments.moment: The Harvard student thought experiment compresses Virgil’s cosmic jealousy into a teacher watching a student outrun him.
signature_moments.source_phrase: oh i'm teaching dante at harvard
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The analogy makes the theological problem feel immediate and human-sized.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang says the Comedy grips because Virgil’s humiliation feels like ordinary human nature rather than mythic abstraction.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's just human nature
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The packet converts a theological scene into a psychological realism claim about why Dante keeps landing.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil becomes the lamp-bearer who lights the road for others while remaining in the dark himself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: carries the lamp behind him
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the compact image that frames Virgil as both necessary guide and tragic non-participant.

signature_moments.moment: The poem wounds a reader into looking for a preacher, which turns literary dissatisfaction into a road toward Christ.
signature_moments.source_phrase: made you look for a preacher
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang’s most compact account of how pagan epic can become Christian preparation.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil becomes the tragic exception: the work moves everybody except the one who wrote it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it can move everybody except virgil
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The line concentrates the whole father-poet paradox into one humiliating image.

signature_moments.moment: Holy fire leaks out of a weaponized poem anyway, reaching readers the poet himself cannot follow.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the holy fire is so strong that there are things that leak out
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the core metaphysical image Jiang uses to explain literature exceeding authorial corruption.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil is blinded by the very moral compromise that let him turn poetry into empire.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this kind of dissonance blinds the poet
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It fuses political temptation with epistemic blindness in one compact diagnosis.

signature_moments.moment: The tree of gluttony trains hunger by dangling fruit that must never be touched.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's a tree with lots of fruit and the sinners just look at it
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This compresses Jiang’s reading of purgatorial pedagogy: desire is intensified in order to be reordered.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang widens the puzzle from one secret Christian to the whole eagle of history.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this is really confusing now for us
signature_moments.why_it_matters: He deliberately uses Dante’s paradise as a pressure test against narrow gatekeeping theology.

signature_moments.moment: Rhipeus explodes the gatekeeping logic because he predates the institutions that were supposed to be necessary.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this is a huge paradox
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the textual wedge Jiang uses to break Virgil’s rule that only explicit Christians can enter heaven.

signature_moments.moment: The path to heaven is recast as fidelity to the good before it is doctrinally named.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you can still follow your intuition and know what's good and right
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the compact democratic salvation formula the class arrives at.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil would rather burn in hell than admit he is wrong.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he'd rather, again, burn in hell than just to admit he's wrong
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang’s most cutting moral summary of Virgil’s self-excusing stance.

signature_moments.moment: A nearly throwaway Aeneid line becomes the crack Dante pries open into a whole theology of justice.
signature_moments.source_phrase: uniquely the most just of all the trojans
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows Jiang reading Dante as a son using the father’s own words to overturn him.

signature_moments.moment: Dante recognizes his friend only when the voice reignites the memory the face can no longer carry.
signature_moments.source_phrase: his voice made plain to me what his appearance had obliterated
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is one of the sharpest body-memory moments in the source, and it matters for the later soul/shade discussion.

signature_moments.moment: Punishment is renamed solace because longing itself is now aimed toward redemption.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I speak of pain, but I should speak of solace
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The line compresses Jiang’s recurring purgatory logic: suffering matters because it is voluntarily aligned with return.

signature_moments.moment: Purgatory’s clock is altered by tears: Nella’s prayers make Forese drink the wormwood of torment sooner and rise faster.
signature_moments.source_phrase: with her abundant tears, has guided me
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang’s strongest packet on prayer as a real causal force in the afterlife economy.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns Nella into the model of a beloved whose virtue can carry someone else upward.
signature_moments.source_phrase: prayed every day for him
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It expands the poem’s metaphysics into a broader theory of relational salvation pressure.

signature_moments.moment: The poem catches up to the dream so closely that Jiang treats the dream as a live interpretive event inside the seminar.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this is your dream, right?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It makes the class itself part of the source’s metaphysical drama rather than just its audience.

signature_moments.moment: The student ties purgatory to an inventory of the wrongs he has done and a desire to seek redemption.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a way for me to seek redemption
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is a performed example of the text converting literary discussion into self-judgment.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang interprets the dream as an encounter with a field where past, present, and future are stacked at once.
signature_moments.source_phrase: beyond time and space, it's all happening at once
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the clearest metaphysical statement linking the dream discussion to his larger consciousness model.

signature_moments.moment: The student says the dream did not predict the poem so much as arrive at the poem early.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he just turned up to class early
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is a memorable image for Jiang’s non-linear timing model.

signature_moments.moment: The lecture crystallizes the paradox of starving without organs.
signature_moments.source_phrase: How do you starve as a soul?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the conceptual hinge that opens the morphic-field explanation in the next packets.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil’s answer is admitted to be a near-miss, pointing beyond him to Statius.
signature_moments.source_phrase: what's the problem with this explanation? The body is gone
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps Virgil as partial guide whose limits the poem must repeatedly expose.

signature_moments.moment: God smiling on the developed fetus becomes Jiang’s modernized scene of ensoulment.
signature_moments.source_phrase: God can now smile upon it
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is a vivid translation of medieval embryology into his consciousness vocabulary.

signature_moments.moment: The soul is redefined as the body-shaped field rather than a spark inside the skull.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's actually the body itself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is one of the source’s strongest and most reusable metaphysical formulations.

signature_moments.moment: Morphic fields let dead embodiment persist as patterned relation instead of flesh.
signature_moments.source_phrase: that's what we call morphic fields
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The term anchors Jiang’s bridge between Dante, consciousness, and earlier seminar examples.

signature_moments.moment: The fields stop fitting the human body and start fitting heaven itself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: they now bend to fit the divine light
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is Jiang’s clearest image for de-individuated beatitude after the shade-stage.

signature_moments.moment: Hunger after death is declared spiritually real rather than symbolically decorative.
signature_moments.source_phrase: only if it's real, does it have any meaning
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This defends the seriousness of purgatorial suffering against reduction to metaphor.

signature_moments.moment: The soul wants divine light, but the body scatters that hunger across lower objects until we no longer know what happiness is.
signature_moments.source_phrase: our souls, they only long for one thing, which is the divine light
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet’s cleanest statement of Jiang’s hierarchy of desire.

signature_moments.moment: Gluttony becomes a chosen starvation that teaches the soul what it really wanted all along.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's a conscious choice on our part
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps purgatory as voluntary retraining rather than imposed torture.

signature_moments.moment: Fire is no longer punishment but kiln-work: it firms the soul the way heat hardens pottery.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the entire point of fire is to make you firm
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang’s final compression of purgatory as strengthening rather than mere pain.

signature_moments.moment: Dante’s God/nature split is used to guard the soul from reduction to body or world.
signature_moments.source_phrase: nature gives us our bodies, but God gives us our soul
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the closing metaphysical distinction of the lecture and clarifies the whole desire model.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's shorthand for the difference between family origin and the independent person who grows from it.
A Purgatory image Jiang links to inherited original sin and to whether descendants should be condemned by ancestral action.
The dream medium through which truth becomes more vivid than direct sight and speaks inwardly.
Believing in God, mercy, and divine mission without being able to prove them.
Continuing to act justly and lovingly because what one does on earth still matters.
Not mere feeling but action strong enough to pray for another forever.
Corrective stations where a specific vice is purged through an inverted lived experience.
A single genuine act of goodness that can still count toward access to Purgatory.
The soul's sustained commitment to complete self-cleansing once it enters Purgatory.
The inward turn a soul must sustain while ascending Purgatory.
The ranked ordering of terraces once Jiang accepts that higher ascent means less severe sin and greater nearness to Heaven.
The reversal of Inferno's ordering that helps reveal the logic of Purgatory's structure.
Church-mediated payments or arrangements that Jiang treats as a way to reduce time in Purgatory.
Jiang's description of pre-Dante Purgatory as a doctrinal patch for awkward cases rather than a robust world.
Jiang's term for Dante's capacity to flesh conceptual theology into a structured imaginative universe.
Jiang's phrase for Dante's model in which access and participation are open beyond the wealthy elite.
A structure where deeds, repentance, and effort matter more than money or institutional permission.
Jiang's paired standard for why Dante's revised Purgatory coheres with a God of love.
Jiang's shorthand for the upper-terrace sins as love aimed wrongly or in the wrong measure.
A student's approved way of describing the ascent from self-enclosure toward less self-centered attachment.
A Christian frame the class invokes to show Dante's structure aligning with a kingdom open beyond ecclesial favoritism.
The student's way of naming pride as a possible foundational source of the other vices.
Part of the student's approved diagnosis for why the purgatorial vices are structurally connected.
A student's attempt to describe Dante's structure as ordered without making one terrace simply better in every respect than another.
The deeper basis of the sins, defined here as how one takes oneself, one's role, and one's agency.
Jiang's phrase for the governing purpose of Dante's cosmology: keeping choice maximally real at every point.
A political-sounding expansion of Dante's free-will structure that Jiang uses to describe the poem's human stakes.
The poetic-prophetic capacity that lets Virgil perceive sacred structure despite his pagan status.
The beatitude chant heard during ascent, marking mercy as part of the purgatorial progression.
Jiang's shorthand for the incremental removal of the marks of sin as Dante ascends the mountain.
Jiang's practical name for what Virgil supplies: disciplined attention more than novel information.
The heavenly form of common possession where sharing enlarges rather than reduces the good held by each.
Goods that provoke envy because dividing them seems to leave less for each possessor.
Jiang's phrasing for love as the principle that explains Paradise and rightly ordered communal life.
The mode in which Dante receives living interior scenes of wrath and its alternatives while still walking.
Jiang's concise account of the virtues opposed to wrath in the three exempla.
Jiang's phrase for Dante's waking visionary state, distinct from sleep-dreams and from external artwork.
A student-offered mechanism for why the wrath visions press themselves on Dante while he walks.
A student's phrase for the visionary faculty Jiang is trying to theorize beyond ordinary dreaming or art.
Jiang's model that memories are stored and retrieved according to emotional value, shaping identity and perception.
The socially operative map built by memory that situates a person in relation to others.
What makes a memory stick naturally, in contrast to rote retention of isolated facts.
Jiang's shorthand for the neuroscientific claim that conscious thought rationalizes rather than governs action.
The field the class begins to invoke as an alternative to reductive psychological projection.
Jiang's claim that Dante accesses Virgil as a real consciousness rather than inventing him from textual study.
The authorial presence encountered in the Aeneid, distinct from later claims about summoning Virgil in the Comedy.
Not a fragment inside the person but the soul itself, treated as the real self in Dante's model.
The connected cosmic field in which memory and personhood can be stored or accessed beyond the brain.
Jiang's image for the infinite field where memories and emotions are stored outside the brain.
Jiang's term for art and dreaming as devices that intensify access to universal consciousness.
The class's gloss for why fictional characters can still be real within a shared field of persons and patterns.
Jiang's account of authentic artistic vocation as divine election rather than career choice.
What real fiction discloses, making it feel true to readers rather than merely fabricated.
Jiang's metaphor for a being cut off from higher consciousness and reduced to automatic material functioning.
The web-like image Jiang invokes for mutual interpenetration between self, universe, and God.
Jiang's term for the person as a reflective miniature of the larger universe.
Jiang's preferred account of real artistic production: receiving rather than inventing.
The perceptual environment that marks the terrace of wrath and enacts its spiritual condition.
The interlocutor in the smoke of wrath who articulates Dante's free-will and corruption argument.
The spiritual office that becomes corrupt when joined to the sword of temporal authority.
Jiang's metaphysical name here for the divine source whose messengers world-historical writers become.
Jiang's filter for distinguishing prophetic writers from merely successful contemporary authors.
Student shorthand for the writer who transmits divine content rather than showing off technique.
The body's interpretive medium, which can either distort reality or convey divine order more faithfully.
Jiang's phrase for imaginal content that descends from beyond the self instead of being willed by the thinker.
The deliberate, object-oriented form of love that can err by bad aim or bad measure.
Jiang's compact label for upper-terrace sins in which desire fastens onto the wrong good or loves a lesser good wrongly.
The inborn evaluative power that judges and reins in other desires, grounding moral responsibility.
Student phrase for the possessive lover's attempt to convert affection into reciprocal obligation.
Jiang uses the term for a medieval poetic mode in which one praises an unattainable or unavailable woman from afar rather than possessing her.
Jiang uses this for what the soul is at its deepest level, distinguished from contingent choices.
Jiang uses this for what one chooses to do, the action-layer that can cloud one's relation to truth.
Francois invokes Rupert Sheldrake's term for shared patterns or fields that shape how consciousness converges.
Jiang uses the term for soul-like fields that project outward, connect people across dimensions, and can explain rapid interpersonal response.
The purgatorial level where greed is purged by prostration, downward gaze, and captivity of hands and feet.
Statius is glossed as belonging with avarice not because he hoarded, but because wastefulness is treated as the opposite excess that withers into the same vice-structure.
Jiang’s term for the divine energy poetry is meant to carry transparently, even though an author can bend it toward empire.
The supra-temporal field Jiang invokes to explain why dreams, images, and later classroom scenes can line up without ordinary causal sequencing.
Jiang’s name for the body-shaped energy pattern that persists beyond flesh and explains sensory continuity in the afterlife.

This 2026-06-26 lecture explicitly resumes earlier Paradise discussion and uses it as the frame for reinterpreting Purgatory.
On 2026-06-26 Jiang moves from Paradise's moral framework into a procedural account of how Purgatory actually works as admission, punishment, and ascent.
This packet captures a live June 26, 2026 classroom correction where Jiang revises his own first claim about Purgatory's hierarchy in response to student reasoning.
This packet explicitly contrasts Dante's Purgatory with what Jiang presents as the church's year-1300 doctrine of indulgence, loopholes, and undeveloped afterlife concepts.
The lecture's June 26 argument now shifts from diagnosing the church's older loophole model to naming the features Dante must introduce for a coherent cosmology of love.
This part of the June 26 class shifts from institutional critique into a positive structural account of Purgatory organized by love, ego, and Beatitude logic.
By this point in the June 26 discussion, the class is moving from macro-structure and love theory into the causal mechanics of whether pride or ego underlies the other sins.
On 2026-06-26 Jiang explicitly frames Dante's free-will cosmology as historically revolutionary for circa 1300 theology, not merely as a timeless spiritual commonplace.
This is the point in the June 26 class where the structural discussion of love yields back to close reading, and Jiang turns the reading into a larger claim about poetry as prophecy.
Here the June 26 discussion welds a pedagogical claim about guides and focus directly onto Dante's envy passage about goods that shrink or grow under sharing.
The June 26 lecture moves directly from the anti-envy economy of shared love into wrath's exemplars, preserving the idea that purification is a retraining of perception and response.

On 2026-06-26 Jiang turns from wrath's moral content to a live psychological question about how visionary images arrive in consciousness, setting up the later memory discussion rather than treating the canto as static allegory.
The June 26 lecture explicitly links Dante's wrath visions to a contemporary account of memory, emotion, and identity, making the poem a route into Jiang's broader anthropology of perception.
On 2026-06-26 Jiang explicitly roots worldview formation in affective memory and treats that as the basis for social identity and navigation.
This June 26 packet marks a transition from neuroscience language about subconscious control to a more metaphysical account of imagination and literary personhood.
On 2026-06-26 Jiang advances an unusually strong ontological reading of literary character: Virgil is treated as contacted rather than composed.
This June 26 stretch fuses Jiang's own novelist experience with a Dantean metaphysics of soul and cosmic connection, making the lecture unusually autobiographical.
This June 26 packet is where Jiang most explicitly links virtue, vision, art, and fiction to an external storehouse of memory rather than to private brain processes.
The June 26 lecture now extends the summoning theory from Dante and Virgil into a broader theology of vocation, artistic truth, and mechanized damnation.
The June 26 lecture makes timeless access and mutual God-world indwelling explicit before returning to the poem, giving unusual metaphysical density to this class.
This June 26 packet bridges Jiang's universalized visionary theory back into the poem at the exact moment Dante enters wrath's black smoke.
This packet anchors one of the lecture's governing commitments on 2026-06-26: Dante's cosmos only works if free will remains prior to astrological or ecclesial determinism.
This June 26 packet connects Dante's free-will politics to Jiang's hierarchy of prophetic writers, keeping both history and authorship under the same moral-metaphysical frame.
This packet shows students actively internalizing Jiang's June 26 writer-metaphysics and restating it in terms of vesselhood and bodily filtering rather than simple talent or fame.
On June 26 Jiang moves directly from a polemic against prestige writing to Dante's divinely sent fantasy, tightening the contrast between empty polish and genuine revelatory vision.
This packet marks the lecture's shift on June 26 from writerly revelation into the central moral schema of Purgatory, where all sins are reclassified as disorders of love.
This June 26 packet is a hinge: the formal free-will doctrine is immediately re-expressed by Jiang as a conflict between possessive Virgilian love and attentive Dantean love.
On June 26 Jiang sharpens the Virgil/Dante split by making the class track the psychology of rejection, entitlement, and revenge inside bad love.
This packet preserves one of the lecture's most memorable June 26 formulations of bad love: coercive escalation followed by retaliatory mythmaking or condemnation.
This packet records the June 26 lecture's hard-line distinction between Virgilian possessive desire and Dantean nonsexual, self-giving love.
This packet preserves Jiang's June 26 claim that the poem's center is where Dante and Virgil finally divide over love, free will, and the heaven/hell split.
This packet ties the June 26 lecture's love dispute directly to Jiang's vocabulary of absolute versus contingent will and to a stark love/lust distinction.
This packet marks a same-day shift from Virgil's self-justifying sin model into a student-led consciousness map that Jiang partially endorses and extends with Sheldrake-style field language.
This packet records a June 26 classroom experiment Jiang explicitly turns into a metaphysical claim about morphic fields and souls before returning to the text.
This packet carries the June 26 lecture from Canto 18's thought-to-vision transition into the siren dream, now read through Jiang's long-running Virgil-as-seducer frame.
This packet develops the June 26 Virgil-as-siren hypothesis into a stronger identity claim: Dante's dream shows him becoming Virgil.
This packet sharpens Jiang's June 26 interpretation from Virgil-as-siren to a full warning that Dante is inheriting Virgil's distorted love unless divine images correct him.
This packet records Jiang's June 26 shift from father/guide imagery to a sharper competitor model for Virgil, still within the same dream-warning framework.
This packet marks Jiang's June 26 pivot from the dream-warning sequence into a concrete moral anatomy of avarice and ecclesial ambition.
This packet records Jiang's June 26 use of Dante's anti-Capet invective as a live model of political greed spreading from one family root into world disorder.
This packet records Jiang's June 26 setup for the Statius encounter by explicitly forecasting an inversion of Virgil's earlier Sordello vanity scene.
This packet captures the hinge where Jiang's June 26 lecture turns Statius's lines on free will into a sustained investigation of chosen penance.
This packet is a strong June 26 statement of Jiang's view that purgation is chosen self-purification and that Dante's figures can feel summoned rather than merely authored.
This packet sharpens Jiang’s June 26 claim that Dante’s characters are psychologically real enough to feel summoned, especially in Virgil’s involuntary reactions.
This is a strong June 26 formulation of Jiang’s self-deception model: truth persists in the self even when the conscious story is evasive.
This packet introduces a major June 26 theme: Virgil’s poetry can prepare another soul for Christianity even while Virgil himself remains outside that completion.
This packet records a June 26 formulation of Jiang’s theory that a text can contain a salvific pressure stronger than its author’s own explicit commitments.
This packet is a concentrated June 26 statement of Jiang’s literature model: divine content can exceed and even indict the writer who shaped it.
This packet marks Jiang’s transition from the Statius case to a broader June 26 doctrine of salvation that will not stay contained within formal Christian identity.
This packet records Jiang’s June 26 movement from explicit conversion toward a more universal account of salvation through righteousness and intuition.
This packet makes explicit on June 26 that Jiang sees Dante as revising Virgil from inside Virgil’s own textual materials.
This packet begins the Forese encounter, which becomes Jiang’s June 26 bridge from abstract punishment to personal memory and prayer efficacy.
This packet preserves a June 26 statement of Jiang’s intercessory-prayer model, one of the source’s strongest causal mechanisms.
This packet is important for June 26 because Jiang explicitly folds the class’s dream-life into the purgatory reading as evidence of seminar pressure.
This packet records one of the source’s clearest June 26 statements that consciousness can exceed linear time.
This packet marks the June 26 transition from dream/consciousness anecdote into explicit metaphysics of shade and embodiment.
This packet contains a major June 26 metaphysical statement: the soul is a morphic bodily field connected to universal consciousness.
This packet extends the June 26 morphic-field model by distinguishing shade-form, heavenly reintegration, and spiritual hunger.
This packet gives a key June 26 desire-model: bodily life confuses the soul’s single hunger for divine light into many appetites.
The source closes on June 26 with two durable formulations: purgatorial fire as hardening and the body/soul split between nature and God.
